subject: ideal point model with group level predictor

messages.author: 14adace15876e095
messages.subject: ideal point model with group level predictor
parts:
Hi list,

Below you may find code for a simple ideal point model with two group level predictors (predictors for the ideal point).

Two things are bugging me:
1) The non-identifiability is handled badly  I believe. I just "added" the group level predictors without worrying about this.
I am not entirely sure what the best way is to go forward.

2) When I run this model, I find estimates for the group-level coefficients with suggest that the data did not affect the prior much. The prior is N(0,2) and the posterior has 2.5% - 97.5% intervals of about -4, +4 (for both parameters)
This puzzles me a bit given that if I estimate the classic 2PLM and I estimate a regression on the estimated ideal point and the predictors then at least I find significance for both predictors.


This is the code:


stan.code.hier1 <- '

data {
int<lower=1> J; // number of abilities
int<lower=1> K; // number of items
int<lower=1> N; // number of observations: complete obs
int<lower=1,upper=J> jj[N]; // ability index for observation n
int<lower=1,upper=K> kk[N]; // item index for observation n
int<lower=0,upper=1> y[N]; // outcome of observation n
real pred4[N]; // value of observation n of the group level predictor
real pred5[N];
}
parameters {
real<lower=0> beta[K];  // constrain discrimination to be positive; also in true data the case
real alpha[K];          // K difficulties
vector[J] theta;        // J abilities
vector[2] gamma;  //real gamma;        
}
transformed parameters{
vector[N] y_hat;
for(i in 1:N)
y_hat[i] <- beta[kk[i]]*(gamma[1]*pred4[jj[i]] + gamma[2]*pred5[jj[i]] +
 theta[jj[i]] - alpha[kk[i]]);
}
model {
alpha ~ normal(0, 4); 
beta ~ normal(0, 4);
theta ~ normal(0,1);
gamma ~ normal(0,2);
y ~  bernoulli_logit(y_hat);
}'


Thanks for all the input.
Louis

Hi Louis,

The part of your model that I'm having trouble understanding is your transformed parameters block:

transformed parameters{
  vector[N] y_hat;
  for(i in 1:N)
    y_hat[i] <- beta[kk[i]]*(gamma[1]*pred4[jj[i]] + gamma[2]*pred5[jj[i]] +
                                       theta[jj[i]] - alpha[kk[i]]);
}

I understand that pred4 and pred5 represent group-level predictors, but it seems these vectors should be indexed by i within the loop rather than by jj[i]. If you want to index by jj[i], the vectors should be of length length J, rather than length N. Try rerunning the model with this transformed parameters block:

transformed parameters{
  vector[N] y_hat;
  for(i in 1:N)

Also, why not estimate the group-level standard deviations for beta, theta and alpha, rather than setting them at fixed values 4, 1 and 4, respectively, like on page 49 and 50 of the manual?

Rob

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: ideal point model with group level predictor
parts:
> On Dec 1, 2014, at 1:52 PM, Rob Trangucci <robert.t...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> ...

>
> transformed parameters{
> vector[N] y_hat;
> for(i in 1:N)
> y_hat[i] <- beta[kk[i]]*(gamma[1]*pred4[i] + gamma[2]*pred5[i] +
> theta[jj[i]] - alpha[kk[i]]);
> }
>
> Also, why not estimate the group-level standard deviations for beta, theta and alpha, rather than setting them at fixed values 4, 1 and 4, respectively, like on page 49 and 50 of the manual?
>

Identifiability.

The IRT problem has a multiplicative and additive invariance that
need to be controlled. Pinning one of the priors, such as theta,
to a unit normal fixes the scale and location of that parameter. That
fixes the scale of beta, so you can let alpha have a mean other than 0
or equivalently add an intercept.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: ideal point model with group level predictor
parts:
Hi Rob,

Thanks for the suggestion. Your remark seems correct. As for the comment on estimating the variances,
I wanted to start with  simple model where the variances are reasonable. I prefer to keep the ideal points at N(0,1) as it is by far the most popular approach. Combined with a sign constraint on beta I get global identification, however this still leaves potential for letting estimating the variances on alpha and beta.

Thanks a lot for the input.

Louis
